preamble: Backing of the voiced dental fricative [ð] to the voiced velar fricative [ɣ] is the defining change of late Gaelic: Old and Middle Irish lenited and non-initial d (spelled ḋ/dh) was [ð], but between the 13th and 18th centuries all dental fricatives were lost across the Goidelic languages, broad [ð] merging with lenited g as [ɣ] and slender [ðʲ] with [ʝ]. As a result, Modern Irish and Scottish Gaelic pronounce the spellings dh and gh identically: dhá [ɣɑː] 'two', dhuit /ɣɞtʲ/ 'to you', Scottish Gaelic modh /mɔɣ/ 'manner' < Old Irish mod /moð/.

examples.from: Old Irish dá 'two', lenited form pronounced with [ð-]
examples.note: The lenited numeral, used attributively before nouns, now begins with the velar fricative; dh and gh are no longer distinguished.
Lenited variant of duit /d̪ˠɪtʲ/; Old Irish lenited d was [ð].
The standalone counting form carries lenition, and its initial dh is pronounced [ɣ], identical to gh.
Non-initial Old Irish d was already the fricative [ð]; the broad fricative is now velar.
